sections.skill: Give an automated workflow only the access its task needs

questions.prompt: What does least access mean?

choices.text: Only the access a task needs

questions.correct_answer: Only the access a task needs
questions.intro: The principle of LEAST ACCESS (also called least privilege) says: give an automated workflow or agent only the access its task needs, and no more. An agent that summarizes your calendar needs to READ the calendar, not delete events or send email. Limit what it can see (one folder, not your whole drive), what it can do (read, not write), and how long access lasts. If something goes wrong, such as a bug or a malicious instruction hidden in a document, least access limits the damage. Review and remove access that is no longer needed.

sections.skill: Compare least access with giving a house sitter keys

questions.prompt: Which key does a plant-watering house sitter need?

choices.text: Every key you own, so the house sitter never gets locked out of any room or vehicle

questions.correct_answer: The front door key
questions.intro: A house sitter who waters your plants needs the FRONT DOOR key. They do not need the key to your safe, your car or your office. If the front door key is lost, the damage is limited. Giving them every key "just in case" means one mistake could expose everything. Least access for software works the same way: give each automation only the keys its job needs, and take them back when the job is done.

sections.skill: Resist convenience and reduce injection damage

questions.prompt: Why do people often grant too much access?

choices.text: Because tools cannot work at all unless they have access to everything on the account
Because it is required by law

questions.correct_answer: "Allow all" is faster than choosing
questions.intro: Convenience pushes toward too much access: clicking "allow all" is faster than choosing. Watch for requests broader than the task, such as a meeting summarizer asking to send email as you. Use separate, limited accounts for automation where possible, never share your main password with a tool, and prefer access that can be revoked (taken back) easily. Prompt injection, instructions hidden in content the agent reads, is much less dangerous when the agent cannot take harmful actions.
